prompt_free_text:
This paper proposes a self-supervised pretraining framework, CET-MAE, for joint EEG-text representation learning, and a downstream decoding framework, E2T-PTR, that transfers the pretrained EEG-side representations into a BART-based EEG-to-text generator. The central idea is to combine cross-modal contrastive alignment with intra-modal masked reconstruction for both EEG and text, while also augmenting the EEG input with a sentence-level EEG token to compensate for missing or misaligned word-level EEG segments in ZuCo. Empirically, the paper reports improved BLEU and ROUGE scores over prior EEG-to-text systems on several ZuCo task combinations.

Overall, the paper addresses an interesting and timely problem. EEG-to-text decoding is still a very immature area, and the attempt to move beyond EEG-only pretraining toward explicit EEG-text pretraining is well motivated. The combination of contrastive alignment and masked modeling is also a sensible design choice, given analogous successes in vision-language and audio-visual learning. The paper is strongest in its high-level motivation and in showing that some form of multimodal pretraining appears beneficial for downstream EEG-to-text generation. The inclusion of ablations comparing contrastive-only, masked-only, and combined objectives is also useful.

That said, I have substantial concerns about the rigor of the experimental validation, the clarity of the methodological description, and the strength of the claimed advances. In its current form, I find the paper promising but not yet fully convincing as a top-tier conference submission.

The main positive aspect is the problem framing. The authors correctly identify two real gaps in prior work: first, the lack of a unified pretraining strategy that jointly captures cross-modal alignment and within-modal structure; second, the under-exploitation of pretrained language models in EEG-to-text decoding. The proposed CET-MAE/E2T-PTR pipeline is conceptually coherent: pretrain a multimodal encoder with reconstruction and contrastive losses, then transfer the EEG-side modules into a text generator. This is a reasonable and potentially impactful direction. I also appreciate the explicit discussion of word-level EEG corruption and missing fixations in ZuCo, and the attempt to address this by appending sentence-level EEG features.

However, the novelty should be calibrated more carefully. The paper presents CET-MAE as the “first pre-trained EEG-text model for EEG-based language decoding,” which may be directionally true in this exact formulation, but the broader idea of aligning neural signals with language using pretrained language models, contrastive objectives, or reconstruction is not entirely new. Prior work such as EEG2Text, C-SCL, BELT, and UniCoRN already explores various forms of language-supervised or alignment-based learning from cognitive signals. The paper’s true novelty is better described as a specific multimodal SSL instantiation for EEG-text with combined masked modeling and contrastive learning, rather than a fundamentally new paradigm. Framing it more modestly would improve credibility.

My biggest concern is that the empirical gains are relatively modest in the most directly comparable settings, while the paper sometimes overstates them. For example, on the 3-task setting against DeWave, BLEU-4 improves from 8.22 to 8.99 and ROUGE-1 F from 30.69 to 32.61. These are real gains, but not dramatic. The abstract’s claim of outperforming SOTA by 32.21% in BLEU-4 appears to rely on relative percentage improvement over a particular baseline and is potentially misleading without context. In the 4-task setting, the comparison to C-SCL is mixed, and in some BLEU metrics the proposed method is slightly worse. In the 5-task setting, the comparison is only against a reproduced EEG2Text baseline, not against all recent methods. Given the small dataset sizes and likely high variance, the absence of statistical significance testing or confidence intervals is a serious omission. Without multiple runs, standard deviations, or significance tests, it is difficult to know whether the reported improvements are robust.

Relatedly, the fairness of the comparisons is not fully established. The paper compares across settings with different numbers of training samples and sometimes against reproduced baselines rather than published numbers. It is not always clear whether preprocessing, token postprocessing, decoding settings, and train/validation/test splits are identical across methods. The note about retaining or removing consecutive repeated words is especially concerning, because such postprocessing can materially affect BLEU. The paper should standardize evaluation protocols and report all methods under exactly the same conditions if it wants to make strong SOTA claims.

A second major concern is possible label leakage or over-reliance on text-side supervision during pretraining and fine-tuning. The paper pretrains on paired EEG-text data using masked text modeling, masked EEG modeling, and contrastive alignment. This is acceptable in principle, but because the downstream task is also EEG-to-text generation on the same benchmark family, the setup is closer to supervised auxiliary-task pretraining than to large-scale self-supervised pretraining in the usual sense. The paper should be much clearer about whether pretraining uses only the training split of each downstream setting, or whether it uses all available paired data from the benchmark before fine-tuning. If any test-set text is involved in pretraining, even indirectly, that would invalidate the results. The current description is too vague on this point.

The “teacher forcing” discussion in the limitations section also raises confusion. The paper states that testing operates with an “implicit understanding” of the ground-truth tokens and later says results depend on teacher forcing. If teacher forcing or any ground-truth conditioning is used at inference time, then the task is not standard EEG-to-text generation and the reported metrics are not directly comparable to unconstrained decoding. If teacher forcing is used only during training, that is standard and should not be described as a limitation in this way. This issue needs to be clarified precisely, because it affects the interpretation of the entire benchmark.

Methodologically, several important details are underspecified. The EEG representation itself is not described clearly enough. What exact features are used per word and per sentence? Are these raw EEG time windows, frequency-band features, or precomputed embeddings from prior work? What is the dimensionality of each token before projection? How are sentence-level EEG features computed and aligned temporally? Since the proposed contribution partly hinges on concatenating word-level and sentence-level EEG, these details are essential. Likewise, the masking strategy for EEG is unusual: sentence-level EEG is “compulsorily masked,” but then also included as an input token in downstream decoding. It would help to explain exactly what the model sees in pretraining versus fine-tuning, and why this does not create a train-test mismatch.

The architecture description is also somewhat ambiguous. The paper says BART is used as a text encoder and that the BART encoder is frozen during CET-MAE pretraining, but later BART is fully fine-tuned in E2T-PTR. How exactly are EEG representations interfaced with BART in the downstream model? Are EEG embeddings fed as encoder hidden states into the BART decoder, or are they fused with textual embeddings in some other way? Is the BART encoder reused at all during downstream decoding, or only the decoder? Figure 2 may clarify this visually, but the text should be self-contained and precise enough for reproduction.

The ablations are helpful but still incomplete. Table 5 shows incremental gains from sentence-level EEG, CET-MAE, and E2T-PTR, but the decomposition is not fully clean. Since E2T-PTR includes both architectural changes and transferred weights, it is hard to isolate whether gains come from pretraining, from the sentence-level token, or simply from increased model capacity. A stronger ablation suite would include: random initialization versus CET-MAE initialization with identical downstream architecture; freezing versus fine-tuning transferred modules; sentence-level EEG token with and without compulsory masking during pretraining; and comparisons against simpler pretraining baselines such as EEG-only MAE or text-conditioned EEG reconstruction without contrastive loss. The current CET vs ET-MAE vs CET-MAE comparison is useful, but the gains are small and again lack variance estimates.

I also found the qualitative examples less persuasive than the paper suggests. Many generated outputs remain heavily influenced by language-model priors and contain hallucinated named entities or semantically plausible but incorrect substitutions. In some examples, the model reproduces long spans correctly but misses the key content words, especially names. This is not surprising given the task difficulty, but it suggests that the model may be relying strongly on generic sentence completion rather than precise EEG decoding. The paper should include stronger analyses to disentangle true EEG-driven decoding from language-model prior completion. For example, one could compare against a text-only prior baseline conditioned on sentence length or task metadata, or evaluate content-word accuracy, named-entity accuracy, and calibration under shuffled EEG-text pairings.

This leads to a broader concern about what exactly is being decoded. ZuCo consists of text-evoked EEG during reading, not imagined speech or intended language production. Therefore, the task is closer to reconstructing read text from neural responses elicited by that text, under strong alignment assumptions and with substantial support from a pretrained language model. This is scientifically interesting, but the paper occasionally overstates the implications for practical BCI communication. Claims about enabling widespread BCI applications for patients with communication impairments should be toned down, especially since the current setup depends on natural reading, eye-tracking alignment, and paired text supervision.

There are also several issues of presentation and writing quality. The manuscript contains many grammatical errors, awkward phrases, and occasional imprecision. Examples include “underrate the proposed framework’s potential,” “does not enter into the text stream,” “the informations interaction,” and inconsistent singular/plural agreement throughout. Some claims are repeated multiple times. The tables are informative, but the narrative around them sometimes overinterprets small differences. The paper would benefit from careful proofreading and tighter exposition.

A few additional technical questions should be addressed. First, how are subjects split between train and test? Is this subject-dependent or cross-subject evaluation? Generalization across subjects is crucial in EEG decoding, and the paper does not foreground this enough. Second, how sensitive are results to the loss weights lambda_T, lambda_E, and lambda_CL? Third, why is the multi-stream transformer only one layer while the EEG encoder is much larger? Fourth, what decoding strategy is used for generation—beam search, greedy decoding, length penalty? Fifth, what computational cost does CET-MAE add relative to directly fine-tuning EEG2Text-style models? These details matter for assessing practicality and reproducibility.

Despite these concerns, I do think the paper has merit. The idea of multimodal EEG-text pretraining is worthwhile, and the reported gains, though modest, suggest the direction is promising. The sentence-level EEG augmentation is also a practical idea for handling missing word-level fixations in ZuCo. If the authors can substantially strengthen the experimental rigor and clarify the setup, this could become a solid contribution.

To improve the paper, I would strongly recommend the following. First, clarify the exact data protocol, especially whether pretraining uses only downstream training splits and whether any form of teacher forcing or ground-truth conditioning is used at inference. Second, report mean and standard deviation over multiple runs, plus significance tests for key comparisons. Third, provide cleaner and more controlled baselines, including identical downstream architectures with and without CET-MAE initialization. Fourth, add analyses that test whether the model truly uses EEG rather than mostly exploiting language priors, such as shuffled-pair controls, content-word accuracy, and named-entity accuracy. Fifth, describe the EEG features, alignment procedure, and BART interfacing in enough detail for reproduction. Sixth, moderate the claims about SOTA margins and BCI impact.

My overall assessment is that this is a promising but currently under-validated paper. The core idea is sensible and potentially useful, but the evidence is not yet strong enough to fully support the breadth of the claims. With stronger methodological clarity, more rigorous evaluation, and more careful positioning, the work could be significantly improved.

Recommendation: weak reject.

Confidence: medium.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes CET-MAE, a self-supervised pretraining framework for EEG-text representation learning that combines masked reconstruction of EEG/text with EEG-text contrastive alignment via a multi-stream encoder. It then introduces E2T-PTR, which transfers the pretrained EEG-side modules into a BART-based EEG-to-text decoder. Experiments on ZuCo reading-task combinations report modest gains over prior EEG-to-text systems on BLEU and ROUGE, and ablations suggest benefits from combining sentence-level EEG features, masked modeling, and contrastive learning.
strengths: Targets an important and challenging problem: open-vocabulary EEG-to-text decoding from non-invasive signals.
The proposed pretraining objective is intuitively motivated, combining cross-modal contrastive alignment with intra-/cross-modal masked reconstruction.
The paper includes several ablations: masking ratios, inclusion of sentence-level EEG features, and comparison against reduced SSL variants (contrastive-only and MAE-only).
Uses publicly known benchmarks (ZuCo 1.0/2.0) and compares against prior methods such as EEG2Text, DeWave, and C-SCL.
Qualitative examples and component-wise analyses help illustrate where the method may help generation quality.
weaknesses: The empirical gains are generally small in absolute terms for the directly comparable settings (e.g., on 3-task data, BLEU-4 improves from 8.22 to 8.99 over DeWave; ROUGE-1 F from 30.69 to 32.61), yet the paper repeatedly frames them as major advances.

Comparisons are not consistently apples-to-apples across methods because training sample counts differ substantially (10710 vs 14407 vs 18791), and some baselines are reproduced while others are taken from prior work with different evaluation conventions.

The paper acknowledges reliance on 'implicit teacher forcing,' but this is a major issue for the claimed decoding setting; the exact train/test protocol and what information is available during decoding are insufficiently clarified, making practical decoding validity hard to assess.

Methodological details are incomplete or ambiguous: exact architecture wiring of the multi-stream encoder, how BART is used in pretraining versus downstream decoding, masking implementation, and loss formulations (especially contrastive loss) are underspecified.
No statistical significance testing or variance across random seeds is reported, despite improvements often being very small (<1 BLEU point).

The evaluation is limited to lexical overlap metrics (BLEU/ROUGE-1) on a small benchmark; there is no semantic evaluation, robustness analysis, subject-wise generalization analysis, or error analysis beyond a few cherry-picked examples.

The use of sentence-level EEG concatenated with word-level EEG may inject strong global information that changes the task definition relative to prior work, but the fairness and implications of this modification are not deeply analyzed.
Writing quality is weak in places, with grammatical issues and several unclear claims, which makes technical verification difficult.
methodological_flaws: A central scientific validity concern is the unclear role of teacher forcing / target-text conditioning. The paper states that during testing the model operates with an 'implicit understanding' of ground-truth tokens, which is conceptually problematic for a decoding task and may substantially weaken the claim of genuine EEG-to-text generation if target-side information influences decoding.

The comparison protocol is not rigorously controlled. Reported SOTA claims mix results from different dataset sizes and evaluation conventions (e.g., repeated-word handling, reproduced vs published baselines), so the headline percentage improvements are potentially misleading.
The paper provides no statistical uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or multi-seed results. Given the small absolute gains, empirical validity is insufficiently established.

The masking-ratio conclusion is not well supported scientifically. The claim that 75% masking is best is based on a narrow trial-and-error sweep without controlling for other hyperparameters or reporting variance; moreover, one table shows 25/25 slightly outperforming 75/75 on BLEU-1, weakening the narrative.

The formula and interpretation of overall EEG masking ratio combine natural missingness with artificial masking, but the scientific implication of treating these as equivalent forms of masking is not justified; natural fixation-missingness is structured noise/misalignment, not random masking.
The transfer-learning ablation (CET vs ET-MAE vs CET-MAE) shows only marginal improvements, yet the paper infers strong complementarity. Without significance tests, these conclusions are overstated.

The paper lacks sufficient mathematical specification of the contrastive objective, pooling strategy, negative sampling, temperature, and reconstruction targets, making the method hard to reproduce and preventing verification of the claimed learning dynamics.

Potential leakage/confounding from using sentence-level EEG features is not adequately analyzed. Since sentence-level signals may encode broad contextual information unavailable in stricter word-aligned settings, improvements may partly stem from changing the input information regime rather than better transferable pretraining.
